title: A swirl of star formation
caption: The starburst galaxy J125013.50+073441.5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: J125013.50+073441.5 · constellation Virgo · about z=0.038 (redshift) away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A glittering swirl sits inside a glowing haze that stretches into space in different directions, forming a fuzzy streak. Bright blue regions sparkle along the arms where new stars are being born. The galaxy has the unpoetic name J125013.50+073441.5, and it is a starburst galaxy, one with an unusually high rate of star formation.

Starbursts teach astronomers a lot about how galaxies and stars evolve. They begin with huge amounts of gas that is turned into new stars. The furious pace is only a phase, and once the gas runs out the star birth slows. Hubble has also captured other well-known starbursts, including the Antennae Galaxies and Messier 82, which forms stars ten times faster than the Milky Way.
The data were gathered with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 for LARS, the Lyman Alpha Reference Sample, which studies how radiation and matter interact in fairly nearby starbursts.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the galaxy in ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light at 336, 438 and 775 nm. The color assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's exposures gather far more light than an eye can.

explore: This galaxy is one of the fourteen LARS targets. The study has described how a type of light called Lyman-alpha emission interacts with nearby gas, which affects how that light escapes into space. The results were published by Hayes, Östlin and colleagues in The Astrophysical Journal in 2013.
alt: A spiral galaxy with bright blue patches along its arms, wrapped in a hazy glow that stretches into a fuzzy streak.
